title: Taiwan Bans AI Chip Exports to China Under US Trade Deal
summary: Taiwan will criminalize unauthorized AI chip exports to China, aligning with US restrictions on Nvidia and AMD hardware smuggling under new trade agreement.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- Taiwan will criminalize AI chip exports to China, adding servers and cutting-edge semiconductors to controlled items list under Foreign Trade Act.
- New measures align with US restrictions and fulfill commitments from the 2026 US-Taiwan Agreement on Reciprocal Trade signed earlier this year.
- Black market smuggling has enabled billions in Nvidia hardware to reach China despite existing US controls on AI accelerators.


Taiwan is implementing sweeping new export controls that will criminalize the shipment of AI chips and servers to China, marking the island's strictest technology safeguard measures to date. Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin confirmed the policy shift aligns with commitments made under the US-Taiwan Agreement on Reciprocal Trade signed in 2026.


## Criminal Penalties for AI Hardware Exports


Under the planned measures, Taiwan will add artificial intelligence servers and cutting-edge semiconductors to its list of controlled items. Shipping restricted AI hardware to China will become a criminal offense prosecutable under the Foreign Trade Act. Currently, Taiwan does not treat unauthorized AI chip exports as a crime, limiting enforcement to warnings and indirect legal charges.


"Going forward, some of our measures on controlled items will correspond to American ones because we have made quite some commitments in the Agreement on Reciprocal Trade," Kung told Bloomberg News in an October 12 interview. He declined to specify an implementation timeline for the new restrictions.


## Closing the AI Chip Smuggling Pipeline


The policy targets a sophisticated black market that has enabled Chinese companies to acquire billions of dollars worth of Nvidia and AMD AI accelerators despite existing US export restrictions. American officials estimate that several billion dollars in Nvidia hardware has reached China over recent years through diversion schemes and unauthorized resellers.


Taiwan's current legal framework only allows authorities to warn potential sellers about violating US rules, with no direct criminal prosecution pathway for chip smuggling. The new measures will provide Taiwanese courts with explicit legal tools to prosecute offenders, closing a significant enforcement gap that smugglers have exploited.


## Strategic Alignment with US Technology Policy


The export controls represent one of President Lai Ching-te's most assertive moves to safeguard Taiwan's technological and national security interests while managing pressure from Washington. Lai previously indicated Taiwan would address US concerns over export controls without providing specific details.


Minister Kung, a key steward of Taiwan's economic relationship with the United States, also announced this week that Taiwan plans to raise $4 billion to develop industrial parks in Texas. These facilities will support a comprehensive domestic supply chain for Nvidia and other AI hardware manufacturers, further deepening US-Taiwan semiconductor collaboration.


## Implementation and Enforcement Timeline


Officially launched on October 16, 2026, through Kung's public statements to Bloomberg News, the policy awaits formal regulatory implementation. Taiwan's government has been exploring expanded legal frameworks since earlier in 2026, when authorities first signaled intentions to criminalize AI chip diversion.


The measures will require amendments to Taiwan's controlled items list and potentially new enforcement protocols for customs and trade authorities. Once enacted, violators could face criminal prosecution under existing Foreign Trade Act penalties, which include fines and imprisonment for unauthorized exports of controlled technologies.


## What This Means


Taiwan's decision to criminalize AI chip exports to China signals a fundamental shift in cross-strait technology policy and reflects deepening US-Taiwan strategic coordination. The move directly challenges China's efforts to acquire advanced AI computing capabilities through gray market channels while positioning Taiwan as a reliable partner in US efforts to maintain technological leadership. As Taiwan simultaneously invests billions in US-based semiconductor infrastructure, the export controls underscore Taipei's commitment to aligning with American technology restrictions even at potential economic cost. The policy sets a precedent for other US allies weighing similar measures to restrict China's access to AI hardware.
